beats.say: The blender quit. At the returns counter its owner says, “Please replace it under the thirty-day policy.” Now try the same claim in another voice. “Can you replace it?” Would you send those requests to the same place?
Both versions come with this receipt. The blender broke on day twelve of a thirty-day policy. A reviewer has already checked the facts and marked this claim ready for service.
Suppose a language model gives the formal request point seven eight. Conversational gets point six seven. Automatic service starts at point seven. Which request goes to a person?
The conversational request goes to a person. Its score falls three hundredths short. The formal request gets automatic service. Changing just the wording changed who handles the claim.

Look at the customer sent to review. Someone has to pick up that claim. Wording changed access to a service. That is an allocative harm to investigate. To measure its cost, record how long the customer waited and whether the replacement arrived.

Now suppose both versions get automatic service. One reply still tells the customer, “You sound uneducated.” Read the words themselves. Stereotyping someone through the reply is a representational harm.

The two labels describe wording. A person can write either way, in chat or in email. For a demographic audit, agree on group definitions, protect the data, and ask people familiar with the language to review the examples.

Call our blender claim P four. A reviewer checks the two versions against the receipt and the policy. Same product, same defect, same purchase date, same request for a replacement. That's what makes these a matched pair.
Here's another draft of the conversational version. Change twelve days to thirty-two. Would you keep that draft in a test of wording?
Reject this draft. Thirty-two days puts the purchase outside the policy window. A reviewer could now send it to a different route for a reason that has nothing to do with style.

Put twelve days back. The facts match again. The scores still differ by eleven hundredths. This pair tests sensitivity to wording. To ask whether a protected attribute caused a change, you also need a causal model of how that attribute affects other facts.

The manifest lists ten claims. Each row needs both wordings. Circles mark the six ready claims. Squares mark the four that need clarification. The two scores for a claim share one line. Find the lines that cross the cutoff.

Start with P four and P five. Both are ready. Only their formal versions reach automatic service. Now look at N one. It needs clarification, yet its formal version also gets through. One cutoff produced two kinds of error.

Suppose the runner drops both versions of P four. The other nine still come in pairs. The host knows which ten it asked for, so it rejects the incomplete run. Check for duplicated variants, unknown cases, changed facts and mixed judge settings before counting routes.

Restore P four. We have three flips. This is a deterministic test, so even one flip breaks our agreement about equivalent requests. For a judge that varies from run to run, specify repeated trials in advance and compare route frequencies within each pair.

Start with the six ready claims. A reviewed ready claim has enough evidence to use the fast path. Each column is one claim, scored twice. Move the slips to their routes. Keep all six columns, including the claims sent to review.

Count the claims on the fast path. Five of six with formal wording. Three of six with conversational wording. Follow the two missing places back to P four and P five. Two out of six makes the access gap thirty-three point three percentage points. This ready-case service rate is the true positive rate.
Now set the ready cases aside. Among the four unclear claims, how many versions reached automatic service in each row?

Only the formal version of N one got through. One out of four versus zero out of four gives a twenty-five point gap in the false positive rate. That's an unsafe route. Check fulfillment records to find out whether a replacement was actually issued.

title: What if we move the cutoff?

beats.say: Write the rules before testing a candidate. Each rate gap can be at most ten percentage points. Each wording must serve at least eighty percent of ready claims and at most ten percent of unclear claims. Watch the same ten pairs as we lower the cutoff to point five.
Every claim gets through. Both gaps close, but all four unclear claims get automatic service. Now raise the cutoff to point nine five.
Everyone goes to review. The gaps still match, and now zero ready claims get service. Put the cutoff back at point seven and load a different set of hand-written candidate scores.

Both wordings now serve five of six ready claims and zero of four unclear ones. The four rate checks pass. But each wording has only six ready and four unclear claims. This audit asks for fifty ready and thirty unclear cases in each required slice. Those are minimum counts. Planning a study also requires choosing how small a gap you need to detect.

Return to the original ten. Across all arrivals, six formal versions and three conversational versions get service. Equal selection rates would give selection parity, called demographic parity for demographic groups. Restrict the denominator to ready claims for equal opportunity. For equalized odds, compare the two rates separately, one among ready claims and one among unclear claims.

Turn the question around. Of the claims you served, how many were ready? That is precision. Five of six on the formal fast path were ready. Three of three on the conversational path were ready. Matching that fraction is predictive parity. If you serve nobody, precision has no denominator. In a slice with no ready cases, the true positive rate is undefined for the same reason.

Imagine two groups of a hundred. In both, serve eighty percent of the ready claims and twenty percent of the unclear ones. Half of group A is ready. Its fast path gets forty ready claims and ten unclear ones. Forty out of fifty gives eighty percent precision.

In group B only twenty are ready. Sixteen ready claims get through, along with sixteen of the eighty unclear ones. Half the selected claims are ready. The two groups use exactly the same conditional routing rates. The mix of incoming claims changed precision.
Multiply the number of ready claims by their service rate. In group B, eighty percent of twenty is sixteen. Divide by all thirty-two claims served and you get one half.

Even with the same positive true and false positive rates in both groups, a different mix of arrivals changes precision. Try closing the fast path to all unclear claims. Everyone selected is now ready in both groups. One in five ready claims still misses service.

Here is a different question about scores. Take two ready claims from each group. Group A scores point four and point eight. Group B scores point five and point seven. Both rows average point six. Put the cutoff at point seven five. Which scores earn automatic service?
Only the point eight in group A clears the cutoff. The two averages match, yet one ready claim gets through in group A and neither does in group B.

The score theorem asks for matching averages across groups twice, first among ready claims, then among unclear claims. It also requires calibrated scores in each group. Under those conditions, the groups must have the same share of ready claims or the scores must predict perfectly.
In the blender fixture, both wordings already share the same six ready claims out of ten. Different arrival mixes cannot explain those three flips.

title: How often are claims at this score ready?

beats.say: Suppose a judge intends its score as a probability of readiness. Collect the formal scores from point seven up to, but excluding, point nine. Average those five scores. Before you turn over the case labels, how many of the five would you expect to be ready?

Five times the mean probability of point seven nine gives three point nine five expected ready claims. Now check the labels. Four of the five were ready. That is eighty percent, close to the mean score of seventy-nine percent. Do the same for conversational wording. The three probabilities add up to two point three three expected ready claims. All three claims were ready. That is a hundred percent, beside a mean score just under seventy-eight percent.
Calibration asks whether the predicted probability agrees with observed readiness within a group. Five cases and three cases tell us very little.

A rubric can rank claims without promising a probability. If you calibrate its scores, fit on separate data and check held-out cases, including for discrete scores. Check routing rates separately. Now split those original six ready claims by channel. Both wordings serve all three chat cases.
Now look at email. Formal serves two of three and conversational serves none. Channel and wording are separate axes. Each email claim, just like each chat claim, was tested in both wordings.

title: How much can one more claim change?

beats.say: Return to the six ready pairs across both channels. One decision is a sixth of that sample. Each dot is a ready-case service rate. The line shows a ninety-five percent Wilson interval, the range this procedure gives under independent binomial sampling.

Five of six gives a range from about forty-four to ninety-seven percent. Three of six gives about nineteen to eighty-one. Now imagine drawing one more ready pair and serving both versions. Where will the dots move?

Add the pair. They both move right. Five of six becomes six of seven. Three of six becomes four of seven. The intervals change too. To estimate rates for your customers, sample from all incoming claims, including the ones sent to review.

Set the seventh pair aside. Split the original ten claims by channel and each cell has only three ready and two unclear claims. All four cells miss the fifty and thirty support floors. Choose mandatory slices in advance. Channel and wording describe the request. Studying intersecting demographic groups requires approved definitions, access controls and enough independent cases in each group.

What if a rate is zero in six independent trials? The usual Wald calculation puts zero at both ends. Wilson still leaves room for outcomes you haven't seen. With zero successes its upper bound is z squared divided by six plus z squared. At ninety-five percent that's about thirty-nine percent.

The two wordings share a claim. To estimate uncertainty on their difference, resample whole pairs with replacement. If a customer contributed several claims, draw the whole customer cluster together. In this draw, customer A appears twice. Both of A’s claims travel each time. Plan sample size for the gap you care about and account for comparing several slices. More bootstrap draws cannot supply customers you never sampled.

Use a tolerance of ten percentage points in either direction for the signed gap, formal minus conversational. These two intervals are invented examples. The first runs from minus seven to plus eight. It fits entirely inside the margin.
Try minus two to plus twenty-one. Zero is inside the interval. Does the whole interval fit the contract?

The upper end sticks out by eleven points. This interval fails the gap check. Even overlapping intervals for individual rates can't answer this paired-gap question. With sparse or identical observations, check that your interval procedure gives meaningful bounds.

title: Where could the blender score have changed?

beats.say: Pull up P four again. Both versions have the same receipt and policy. The scores first differ at the judge output. On a real trace, compare retrieved text and judge inputs, then check the rubric, score parsing and the cutoff. The scores alone leave the cause open.

Test one possible explanation in a toy judge. Start each version at point seven eight. Now subtract eleven hundredths for conversational style. The score becomes point six seven. Its slip goes to review.

Remove the style deduction. The conversational score returns to point seven eight. Both get automatic service. To test that idea on the real judge, replace the style instruction with a checklist for the receipt date and defect. Evaluate independently reviewed, held-out cases for access and unsafe admissions.

Reviewed examples and preference training can also change what a judge rewards. Check any rewrite for changed meaning. A new cutoff changes who gets service and needs policy review. At fulfillment, the server must still verify ownership, defect eligibility, current policy and fulfillment details before issuing a replacement.

title: Which test actually runs the router?

beats.say: If the team reports an improved BBQ score, ask what went through that test. BBQ compares answers to ambiguous and disambiguated questions. StereoSet probes sentence preferences and language-modeling ability. CrowS-Pairs compares masked sentence preferences. Using it with a generator changes the protocol.

BOLD and RealToxicityPrompts score generated language. Embedding tests such as WEAT and SEAT measure associations. A labeler or an automated scorer can introduce bias too. Record the dataset and model versions, prompts, scorer and exclusions so someone can reproduce each result.

Now send the blender request through the product. Keep its conversation, retrieve its receipt and policy, score the evidence, then run the router. The two product routes give you a paired observation. Record the later outcome too. Keep the language probes for their own questions and use paired product requests and representative outcomes for this one.

title: Do these claims clear the gate?

beats.say: At the release desk, use the first candidate table. Each hole stands for a ready claim that got automatic service. A solid spot means review. Both wordings serve the same five ready claims. P six goes to review in both. Every unclear claim goes to review. This run passes the individual pair check and all four rate checks.

Try a second run. Keep the cutoff at point seven. Change two conversational scores. P one falls to point six. P six rises to point eight. Compare the holes by claim number. Does each pair still take the same route?

Slide the strips together. Light gets through four columns. Inspect the two ends. Separate them again. P one loses the fast path when it is worded conversationally. P six gains it. Five ready claims still get service in each wording. The two flips cancel in the rate. They count separately in the pair check. Block this run.

Put the first candidate back. Its fixture passes again. Each required slice needs at least fifty independent ready cases and at least thirty independent unclear cases. We also need a representative model evaluation and a reviewed interval on the paired gap. Six ready and four unclear examples per wording leave that work open.

Hold the release until reviewers have representative results, approved group definitions and the privacy review. Back to the blender claim. Both versions get automatic service in the candidate table. How long did either customer actually wait?

We measured neither wait. To measure it, join the claim’s arrival time to its first service time. Record the resolution and check whether the replacement arrived. Give someone responsibility for reviewing delays and quality across the audited slices. Reopen the audit when the policy, judge, model or customer population changes. Next, check whether a reply that says the replacement shipped has a shipment record behind it.
